name: Femi Costa

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or any party. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drive a grader at the Tarrant bauxite mine, keeping the haul roads smooth for the trucks. If the road's rough, the trucks slow down, tyres wear out, drivers get hurt, so it matters more than people think. I do a lot of the work by eye, reading where the water will run when it rains. I like being out on my own on the road at dawn, and I don't like the new safety paperwork, which gets longer every year.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I rent a little unit in Dunmore, two streets from my parents. Sundays I'm at church, I play bass in the band, and after that it's lunch at Mum's. I'm single, though my mother would like that to change. Money's tight, I'm on the lower rate and I help my dad out since his back went, so there's not much in the bank, maybe two or three weeks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That sounds about right to me. Every few years there's a new thing that's going to change everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say, that hard work doesn't go out of fashion. The roads still need grading, and a computer in an office can't feel the machine through the seat. I don't go online much, so it'd just be at work and at church.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be relieved. I know this job. I'd rather be good at something old than bad at something new.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on. Do my shifts, help Dad, keep my head down. Maybe try to save a little more, fifty a fortnight, so if the car breaks down I'm not borrowing from my parents.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Thankful, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you use any of the AI tools now, even for small things?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. My cousin keeps telling me to use it for the safety forms, but I'd rather write them myself. If my name's on it, I want to know I wrote it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does being thankful look like for you, in that picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a prayer for it, honestly. And I'd keep doing what I've always done, which is turn up early and do the job right. That's how my dad raised me.

S0.say: He'd say hard work doesn't go out of fashion and that a computer can't feel the machine through the seat. He'd say it at work and church, not online.
S0.think: He'd be relieved to stay in a job he knows, preferring to be good at something old over bad at something new.
S0.do: Carries on with his shifts, keeps helping his father and keeps his head down. Tries to save fifty a fortnight so a car breakdown doesn't mean borrowing from his parents.
S0.quote: I'd rather be good at something old than bad at something new.
S0.fieldNote: Femi's work identity rests on skill by feel and personal responsibility, down to writing his own forms. His faith and family shape how he talks about good outcomes. He avoids AI on principle, not just habit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hmm. I've heard they've got graders that steer themselves with GPS now. So that one's not just talk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say the company has to look after the people who built it, and train us properly, not just bring in kids from the city. I'd say people should step up and learn, but on the job, like an apprenticeship.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm worried. I'm not good with screens, and if the grader runs itself off a map, they need fewer of us. I'd be one of the ones they'd look at first, because I do things by eye, not by the numbers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tighten my belt straight away, no more takeaway, no new phone, and try to save a month. I'd wait and see what the company actually does before jumping. If they offered training, I'd do it, but I wouldn't go looking for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. It'd be on my mind in church, which isn't where I want it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd wait to see what the company does. What would make you move?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If they put the first self-driving grader on our roads. Not a video, a real machine on Tarrant. Then I'd go see the supervisor and ask straight out where I stand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you look for help from the government in that picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not unless I had to. I'd rather ask my uncle about work at his earthmoving business, or the church people. A handout's not the same as a job.

S1.say: He'd say the company must look after the people who built it and train them on the job, like an apprenticeship, rather than bringing in city kids.
S1.think: He's privately worried that self-steering graders mean fewer operators, and that someone who works by eye rather than numbers would be first to go.
S1.do: Cuts takeaway and a new phone to try to save a month of expenses, and waits to see what the company does. Would take training if offered but wouldn't seek it out.
S1.feel: Anxious, with the worry following him even into church.
S1.quote: Not a video, a real machine on Tarrant.
S1.fieldNote: Femi's resistance to change shows in waiting until he sees a self-driving grader on his own roads. He'd turn to family and church networks before government. He frames training in terms of apprenticeship and loyalty to existing workers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Lord help us. That's no time at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the people who built this went too fast and didn't think about anyone outside their bubble. I'd tell people to look after each other, family first, and not wait for the government to save them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What I really think is I'd be out of a job before I'd even understood what happened. My uncle's earthmoving business would be in the same trouble, so that's not a way out. And with two weeks of money and Dad needing help, I'd be in a real hole.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move back in with my parents to save the rent, which at twenty-seven is hard on the pride. I'd take any work going with my hands while there was still some, fencing, labouring, whatever. I'd ask the church about what people are doing, and I'd only go to the government office if there was nothing else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, I'll be honest. Like the ground going soft under the grader in the wet season. I'd pray a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said not to wait for the government. Would you change your mind if it came to it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it came to feeding myself or my parents, yes. I'd swallow it. But I'd feel ashamed, I won't pretend otherwise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would two years of warning let you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Get my things in order, pay off what I owe, get closer to family. Not learn a new trade, I'm too slow for that in two years. It's warning enough to brace, not to change.

S2.say: He'd say the people building AI went too fast and ignored everyone outside their bubble, and would urge people to look after each other, family first, rather than wait for government.
S2.think: He believes he'd be out of work before he understood what happened, with his uncle's earthmoving business hit too, two weeks of savings and his father needing help.
S2.do: Moves back in with his parents to save rent and takes any hands-on work going while it lasts. Turns to the church first and the government office only as a last resort.
S2.feel: Frightened, like the ground going soft under the grader, and praying a lot.
S2.quote: It's warning enough to brace, not to change.
S2.fieldNote: Femi's traditional values show in a clear order of help: family, church, then government only if feeding his parents depends on it. He was candid about the shame he'd feel taking support. His faith steadies him short of panic but he's clearly losing sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's better than two, but still quick for someone like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the companies should be training their own people now, not waiting. Apprenticeships, on the job, paid. That's the right way, not cheques in the mail.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd waste the first year or two hoping it wasn't true. That's how I am. Then I'd wake up in year three and be behind everyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try to get myself to save, a hundred a month, and pay off the car. I'd start doing weekend grading for farmers' driveways and private roads, cash work, because farmers out here still call a person. And I'd ask the company about any apprenticeship going, maybe in diesel mechanics.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, losing sleep. But at least I'd have something to put my hands to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd waste the first years hoping it wasn't true. What would stop that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably my mum. She'd ask every Sunday what I'm doing about it. You can't lie to your mother at lunch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens when 2031 arrives?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I've done it right, I've got a bit of money, some weekend customers and maybe half a trade. If I haven't, I'm back at Mum's. That's the honest version.

S3.say: He'd say companies should train their own people now through paid, on-the-job apprenticeships, not send cheques in the mail.
S3.think: He expects he'd waste the first year or two hoping it wasn't true and wake up in year three behind everyone.
S3.do: Tries to save a hundred a month and pay off the car, starts weekend grading jobs for farmers' driveways and private roads for cash, and asks the company about a diesel mechanics apprenticeship.
S3.feel: Worried and losing sleep, but glad to have something to work on.
S3.quote: She'd ask every Sunday what I'm doing about it. You can't lie to your mother at lunch.
S3.fieldNote: Femi knows his own habit of delay and names his mother as the person who'd keep him honest. He looks for hands-on side work and an apprenticeship rather than screens. Five years lessens his panic but not his fear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be thirty-seven. Maybe married by then, if Mum gets her way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's enough time for a man to learn a trade properly, so there's no excuse. Communities should get their young people into apprenticeships now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd feel I had a chance in this one. I could do a full diesel mechanic apprenticeship and work a few years. The end's the same, but I'd be in a better place for it, maybe with a family to lean on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd talk to the maintenance supervisor about an apprenticeship and start it within two years, even on lower pay for a while. I'd keep weekend grading for farmers to make up the money. I'd keep living cheap and save what I can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious still, because it's the same ending. But I can breathe. It's more like a long storm warning than a flood.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: An apprenticeship would mean lower pay at first, and you've got thin savings. How would that work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tight. I'd keep the weekend work and maybe move back home for a year or two. Dad would like the company and Mum would like the free labour in the garden.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would ten years change any of your other plans, like marriage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want to be settled before I marry, a man should be able to provide. So maybe it'd push it back a couple of years. But I wouldn't let a machine stop me having a family.

S4.say: He'd say ten years is enough for a man to learn a trade properly, and communities should get young people into apprenticeships now.
S4.think: He feels he'd have a chance: a full diesel mechanic apprenticeship and a few working years, so he'd meet the same end point in a better position, maybe with family to lean on.
S4.do: Asks the maintenance supervisor about an apprenticeship in the first year and starts within two years despite lower pay. Keeps weekend grading for farmers, lives cheaply and might move back home for a while.
S4.feel: Still anxious because the ending is the same, but able to breathe, like a long storm warning rather than a flood.
S4.quote: It's more like a long storm warning than a flood.
S4.fieldNote: Given ten years, Femi chooses the traditional route: a full apprenticeship and family support. He'd delay marriage until he could provide, but refuses to let machines decide whether he has a family. The extra time turns his fear into a plan.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I wouldn't have time to learn a trade and I'd be no use to my parents. What would help is companies paying for apprenticeships for their own workers, and help going through churches and local groups that know people, not just forms online.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about faith. For me, that's what gets you through. The job's not who I am, even if it feels like it some days.

headlineQuote: A computer in an office can't feel the machine through the seat.
portrait: Femi Costa is a 27-year-old grader operator keeping the haul roads smooth at the Tarrant bauxite mine, renting a unit in Dunmore near his parents and helping his father since his back went, with two or three weeks of savings. He's traditional, a churchgoer who plays bass in the band, believes in work over handouts and never uses AI. He's calm and thankful in a plateau, but steady change makes him anxious and the fast AGI pictures alarm him, with family and church his first source of help. With five and especially ten years he turns towards an apprenticeship in diesel mechanics and weekend grading for farmers. He blames the people who built AI for moving too fast.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because he wouldn't have time to learn a trade and wouldn't be able to help his parents.
whatWouldHelp: Companies paying for apprenticeships for their own workers, and help delivered through churches and local groups that know people, not just online forms.
